description: Learning cards with subtitle, body paragraphs, and takeaway per card.

cards.title: If You Have to Explain It, It's Broken
cards.subtitle: You watch someone reach for your product, then stop and look around for help.
body: They didn't open your app to learn. They opened it to do something. The pause happens before they even try.
Hesitation is confusion wearing a polite face. People skip instructions when they're already moving.
cards.takeaway: The moment you need to explain is the moment you already lost.

cards.title: Clarity Beats Cleverness
cards.subtitle: You designed a hidden gesture that feels like magic. Users swipe right past it every time.
body: The shortcut that seemed playful in the prototype now just confuses people who want to move forward.

• Dull choices feel safe when you're rushed
• Clever choices feel risky when you're uncertain
• That clever moment becomes the place where they give up
cards.takeaway: You designed it to impress yourself, not to get out of the way.

cards.title: The Object Should Tell You What to Do
cards.subtitle: They push the door. It says pull. They try again, harder.
body: The handle looks like something you grab and pull, so they pull. But the door was designed to push.
Shape tells people what to do before they think. When form lies, people trust themselves less.
cards.takeaway: Physical shape is instruction—make it honest.

cards.title: Errors Are Designed In
cards.subtitle: Seventeen people this week hit delete instead of save. You blame them for not being careful.
body: The buttons sit next to each other, same size, same color. The system baited them into clicking wrong.
When the same mistake repeats, it's a feature you didn't plan for.
cards.takeaway: Blaming users for predictable behavior is just expensive denial.

cards.title: Feedback Is How Systems Speak
cards.subtitle: You tap submit. Nothing happens. You tap again. Now you've submitted twice.
body: The system was processing the first tap, but it never told you. So you guessed, acted, and broke something.

• Silence doesn't feel like patience
• It feels like failure
• No signal makes people repeat the action
cards.takeaway: Bad news is still better than nothing.

cards.title: People Don't Read Your Manual
cards.subtitle: They click three things, decide how it works, and never update that mental model again.
body: You built it one way. They guessed another. Now they're using your product wrong, and they'll keep using it wrong.
Users build their theory while moving, not while reading. The wrong model sticks harder than the right one.
cards.takeaway: The gap between what you meant and what they learned is permanent.

cards.title: Signifiers Are the Real Instructions
cards.subtitle: The door opens both ways. The handle only exists on one side. Everyone pulls.
body: It can push and pull, but the handle screams pull. That's a signifier lying to you.
Affordances are what's possible. Signifiers are what gets tried. You're designing what it looks like it does.
cards.takeaway: People don't read affordances. They read signals.

cards.title: Constraints Make Things Easier
cards.subtitle: You flip the USB plug three times before it finally fits. Now it only goes in one way.
body: The old plug gave you two chances to be wrong. The new one removes the choice entirely.
Constraints aren't restrictions. They're decisions made upstream so you don't have to.
cards.takeaway: The best constraint is the one you don't notice because the wrong thing was never possible.

cards.title: The Gulf Between Wanting and Doing
cards.subtitle: You know what you want to do. You just can't figure out how to make the system do it.
body: There's the goal in your head and the maze of buttons in front of you. Somewhere between the two is a translation you can't figure out.

• Small gaps feel natural
• Large gaps feel like the product is fighting you
• The distance is measured in abandoned attempts
cards.takeaway: Good design closes the gap before you notice it existed.

cards.title: What You Can't Find Doesn't Exist
cards.subtitle: You spent two weeks building the export feature. No one uses it because it's buried in settings.
body: They looked for it once, didn't see it, and decided your product can't do exports. The feature works perfectly. It's just invisible.
People scan for five seconds, then decide what's possible. Now you're getting feature requests for something you already built.
cards.takeaway: If it takes more than two clicks to discover, it's not a feature. It's a secret.

cards.title: Slips and Mistakes Are Different Problems
cards.subtitle: You reach for save and hit delete. Then you confidently choose the wrong workflow entirely.
body: The first one is a slip—your hand misfired. The second is a mistake—your mental model was wrong from the start.
You fix slips with better buttons. You fix mistakes with better explanations.
cards.takeaway: Most products only defend against one and wonder why the other keeps happening.

cards.title: Put the Knowledge in the World
cards.subtitle: The pilot forgets a step mid-flight. The checklist doesn't. The plane lands safely.
body: Memory is fast when it works and useless when it fails. Labels, signs, and checklists don't forget.
That's why cockpits rely on paper, not recall. Memory is unreliable under pressure.
cards.takeaway: Visible information never fails.

cards.title: When Everyone Fails, It's the System
cards.subtitle: Fifty people this month made the same error. You keep blaming the users.
body: One person makes a mistake, maybe they weren't paying attention. Fifty people make the same mistake, and you're still calling it human error.
That's not carelessness. That's the system teaching them to fail.
cards.takeaway: One failure is an accident. Repeated failure is design.

cards.title: Good Design Disappears
cards.subtitle: You opened a hundred doors this year. You remember the one that stuck.
body: The doors that worked didn't even register. You just walked through. The one that confused you, that one stays in memory.

• Good design earns nothing
• Bad design earns a reputation
• Things that work don't get noticed
cards.takeaway: The best design feels like no design at all.

cards.title: Controls Should Mirror the Thing They Control
cards.subtitle: Four burners in a square. Four knobs in a row. You turn the wrong one and burn your hand.
body: The burners are arranged like a grid, but the knobs are lined up like a queue. Now every time you cook, you're translating spatial logic.
Good mapping makes the connection obvious. Bad mapping forces mental translation every single time.
cards.takeaway: You keep guessing because the layout keeps lying.

cards.title: Make the Dangerous Thing Hard to Do
cards.subtitle: The microwave door is open. You press start. Nothing happens. You're annoyed, but not burnt.
body: The interlock feels like friction until you realize what it just prevented. A car that won't shift out of park without the brake.
These aren't obstacles. They're guardrails at the exact moment you're most likely to wreck.
cards.takeaway: Annoyance now beats catastrophe later.

cards.title: Memory Is the Wrong Storage System
cards.subtitle: You ask users to remember six options. They show up distracted and forget three.
body: They're not focused. Working memory holds maybe four things, and it's already holding what they had for lunch and where they parked.

• Memory is tiny and already busy
• Recognition beats recall every time
• If your design depends on memory, it depends on luck
cards.takeaway: Show, don't ask them to remember.

cards.title: Complexity and Confusion Are Not the Same
cards.subtitle: A pilot flies a plane with a thousand switches. You can't figure out your TV remote.
body: The cockpit is complex because flying is hard. The remote is confusing because someone organized eight buttons poorly.
Complexity lives in the task. Confusion lives in the design. Complex systems can still feel clear.
cards.takeaway: The goal isn't to remove complexity. It's to stop creating confusion.

cards.title: Symptoms Lie, Root Causes Hide
cards.subtitle: Users keep hitting the wrong button. You make the label bigger. They still hit the wrong button.
body: The symptom was the mistake. The root cause was why the button was confusing in the first place.
The first explanation is always the visible one. The real problem is usually three layers deeper.
cards.takeaway: Now you're just patching symptoms faster than they appear.

cards.title: Design for the Person Who Isn't Paying Attention
cards.subtitle: Your user is on a phone call, holding coffee, and walking. They're not reading your tooltip.
body: They're not giving you their full attention because they never had it to give. They're tired, distracted, or just passing through.
You designed for someone focused and calm. That person doesn't exist.
cards.takeaway: Design for the exhausted user. The alert one will be fine.
